correctness.rationale: The XOR graph has parameters (16,5,0,2); the open neighborhoods used for the main theorem are those of its ten-regular complement. Independent replay produced the sixteen distinct ten-vertex facets, 11,804 nonempty faces, 4,780 collapse pairs and 1,050 toggle pairs. All 65,680 covers sort acyclically; using the globally reversed arrow convention in the frozen verifier does not alter acyclicity. The critical cells are one vertex, six 3-cells and 137 4-cells. Integral signed Morse elimination reproduces the stated minor on columns 2,4,9,10,23,26 with determinant +1. The six corresponding 4-cells together with the 3-skeleton have a unimodular integral degree map and form an acyclic simply connected, hence contractible, CW subcomplex. The other 131 attaching maps to that subcomplex are null, giving the exact wedge of four-spheres. The dominance condition is that no closed C-neighborhood is wholly in a face; complementing shows D(C)^∨ = N(H). Combinatorial Alexander duality on 16 vertices gives degree 16−4−3=9 in D(C) and no other reduced integral homology. The argument does not infer its homotopy type from its homology.

evidence: The prior matching has 26,799 pairs, one critical singleton {0}, and 131 critical sets of size ten. Add the pair (empty,{0}); the singleton is then a sink, so no cycle is created. Independent replay of the earlier increasing-pivot stages via the closed-neighborhood predicate reproduced all stage counts and sorted all 53,731 augmented faces through 401,104 arrows, leaving just the 131 size-ten critical sets.

Taking complements reverses all directed arrows and gives an acyclic matching on the nonfaces of N(H) in the full 15-simplex, with 131 critical sets of size six. Faces of N(H) never have outgoing edges to nonfaces, since all crossing covers point down.

To see the relative implication directly, group the matched nonfaces into two-face blocks and leave critical nonfaces as singleton blocks. A directed cycle of blocks would have one dimension drop for each edge between blocks and so would have to use a rise through the matched arrow in every block, lifting to a cycle in the original digraph. In reverse topological block order, starting from N(H), each two-face block is an elementary expansion and each singleton attaches a 5-cell, since all other required subfaces are already present. Such steps preserve components and homotopy groups through degree three. The final full simplex is contractible, so N(H) is 3-connected. Integral Alexander duality gives its only reduced homology Z^131 in degree four. Hurewicz realizes a basis by maps of four-spheres, and homology Whitehead gives the claimed wedge equivalence.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: The prior homotopy statement directly implies the dominance corollary and its certificate supplies the connectivity needed to lift dual homology to the main homotopy result. Neither an unavailable source nor the false rule that Alexander duality preserves homotopy is used.

For a set T of vertices, T is in D(C)^∨ exactly when T is not a dominating set of C, equivalently some x has T disjoint from N_C[x]. This says T is contained in the open H-neighborhood of x.

originality.rationale: The archived dominance result 0b2c4cb32b46 explicitly proves the stronger dominance homotopy type for the identical graph. Combinatorial Alexander duality transfers the homology but not, by itself, the open-neighborhood homotopy type. However, the actual prior proof provides a complete acyclic face matching. Complementing its pairs yields a relative matching on the missing faces of N(H) in the full simplex, with only 131 critical 5-cells. This implies the necessary 3-connectivity and hence the four-sphere wedge. Thus the prior exact certificate, not merely its stated homology or an analogous graph, covers the main result by a direct inference.
residual_risks: The assessment establishes existing mathematical coverage from the exact matching, not a claim that the older record explicitly phrases the dual homotopy theorem or that it was first discovered there.
